newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Czech Social Democrats seek unity at conference.
newsitem.headline: Czech Social Democrats seek unity at conference.

text.p: The people in Tirana were in shock on Friday, fearing the country's downward slide into anarchy will get worse before it gets better and can only be solved by outside intervention.

"We can't comprehend what has happened here," one young woman said after the orgy of looting of weapons that has left civilians across the country armed to the teeth and the army and police disintegrated.
In the dusty capital whose pot-holed roads bear testimony to four decades of Stalinist rule, you can buy a Kalishnikov automatic rifle for $3 but chances of getting a potato are slim.

Food stores and warehouses were emptied on Thursday in a wave of panic buying and looting by civilians making early use of weapons seized from army barracks in the capital and other towns across the country.

"There are no potatoes, eggs, apples, cheese or bread, not in the shops or in the warehouses," said the lone stall-holder in Tirana's main open market as he offered his last stock of nuts, with no new supplies expected.
"We are afraid of getting looted," he said as he surveyed his meagre stock.
"The situation is terrible, the only hope for us is Europe, if we had peacekeeping troops, people will hand in their arms."
The Albanian government said earlier this week it had appealed to European members of NATO to send in peacekeepers to organise the surrender of weapons from civilians.

All but a couple of the wholesale food stores were closed. At one of the few still open a lorry-driver was unloading potatoes and onions brought from neighbouring Greece, after running the gauntlet of armed looters who fired at the truck.
Indicating the bullet holes in the side of the vehicle, he said that despite the danger he would make another trip, "because we have to eat".
He said the business was profitable since Albanian customs officials had vanished, meaning he did not have to pay the normal 30 per cent import duty they demand.

A young man insisted on conducting discussions under shelter for fear of falling bullets from wild shooting in the air that has caused three deaths and over 70 injuries in the capital from falling bullets, many of which lie scattered in the city's streets.
"We need to be armed, because everyone else is armed," he said," adding that he had obtained one gun -- "one is enough".
"I want a weapon in case we get attacked, by thieves, or someone trying to rape my wife or sister," he said. "We are very, very frightened."
"If we don't get peace-keeping troops from abroad, Albania is finished."

Asked whether he wanted the resignation of President Sali Berisha, demanded by anti-government rebels in the south because he failed to stop savings schemes that bankrupted thousands, he said the right-wing leader should go, but only when the authority of the state had been restored.
The gloomiest prediction came from a middle-aged man pushing a bicycle loaded with a huge sack of potatoes, who said things were bound to get worse.
"If they are shooting in the air today they will be shooting at each other tomorrow," he said. "When someone is killed there will be revenge killings, there could be civil war."

"There is no real reason for a civil war here, but in Albania these things can spread very easily," a veiled reference to the traditional Albanian code of vendetta where inter-family feuds are carried through generations.
